articles.title: Immanuel Feyi-Waboso: Exeter Chiefs winger should be fit for England's Nations Championship campaign
articles.summary: England winger Immanuel Feyi-Waboso should be fit to feature in next month's Nations Championship matches.
articles.body:
England winger Immanuel Feyi-Waboso should be fit to feature in next month's Nations Championship after a scan on a hamstring injury revealed a positive prognosis.

Feyi-Waboso missed this year's Six Nations after hurting his hamstring in January but has started every league game for Exeter this season - although he will be absent for Sunday's European Champions Cup trip to French champions Toulouse.

He was a key part of all three of England's Nations Championship games over the summer and crossed for tries against Fiji and Argentina.

"How he's reporting on it post-game and yesterday [Tuesday] there's nothing I'm hearing from our physios saying there should be a long-term issue," Exeter director of rugby Rob Baxter told BBC Sport.

"Had a scan, he's got some awareness there.

"The scan doesn't show up too much. It's one of those things, scans tend to always show something, but actually on testing he's very good.

"So we're hopeful that we can kind of almost treat the symptoms he's showing and see where he gets to over the next week or so."

Exeter examine extent of Feyi-Waboso injury

As a centrally contracted England player, national team officials have the final say over Feyi-Waboso's treatment.

He has been assessed by an England physio, with Steve Borthwick's side due to play the first of their final three Nations Championship games against Australia at Twickenham's Allianz Stadium on 8 November.

"We're in a delicate time for both parties, aren't we - it's a delicate time for us and a delicate time for England," added Baxter.

"We're desperate for Manny to play because we've got some important games and England want him to be able to feature in the autumn.

"Hopefully there won't be any dispute based on we'll just work on where Manny functionally is, how he feels he is, and we'll take it that way."

Feyi-Waboso's injury could not have come at a worse time for Exeter.

The Chiefs are without all four of their first-choice options on the wing for the trip to Toulouse, with the England winger joining Campbell Ridl, Olly Woodburn and Paul Brown-Bampoe in the treatment room.

Tommy Wyatt played on the left wing against Newcastle while Ben Hammersley came on to replace Feyi-Waboso on the right, with Sam Harris making his first Prem start for Exeter at full-back.

"We are a little stretched there, but then we've still got guys who've got Premiership experience," said Baxter.

"Tommy Wyatt, Ben Hammersley, obviously Sam Harris has played some rugby for us now, so we've still got some options.

"Zack Wimbush we've utilised on the wing before, Nick Lilley has played Premiership rugby on the wing before, so although they wouldn't be classed as out-and-out wingers, we have had a few guys who we've deployed on the wing."

articles.title: British and Irish Lions Women: Cardiff's Principality Stadium to host team's first-ever match against France
articles.summary: The British and Irish Lions Women's team will play their first ever match against France on August 27 in 2027; The match will take place at the Principality Stadium in Cardiff before they head on their first ever Tour to New Zealand
articles.body:
The Howden Lions Women's Cup will provide supporters with their first opportunity to see Jo Yapp's side in action on home soil ahead of the inaugural Tour to New Zealand in 2027. The Tour begins Saturday September 4 when the Lions Women face a Black Ferns XV at Semenoff Stadium in Whangārei, before the historic first Test against the Black Ferns at Go Media Stadium in Auckland on Saturday September 11.

The Lions will then take on an Invitational XV at FMG Stadium Waikato in Hamilton on Tuesday September 14, with the second Test in Wellington on Saturday September 18. The Series concludes with the third and final Test at One NZ Stadium in Christchurch on Saturday September 25.

British and Irish Lions Women's Head Coach, Jo Yapp, said: "There are moments in sport that only come around once - and this is one of them.

"For our British and Irish Lions Women's team to step onto the field for the first time, on home soil and in front of our fans, is going to be incredibly special.

"France are the ideal team for an occasion like this. They bring a relentless defence and a real edge in attack. That's exactly the challenge that we need before heading to New Zealand.

"I'd love to see everyone get behind the squad and share this milestone with us. It will be a moment in history."

Ben Calveley, CEO of The British and Irish Lions, added: "We're immensely proud to announce our first-ever British & Irish Lions Women's fixture, in what is a monumental moment in Lions history.

"The Principality Stadium is a special venue with a rich rugby heritage, and it provides a fitting stage for such an occasion.

"With regards to our opposition, France are an outstanding side with a wealth of talent and experience, and they will present a huge test for Jo and her squad.

"We want to put on a show and create a spectacle of the highest level, both on and off the pitch. Our ambition is to provide an opportunity for the fans to be part of a truly special day."

articles.title: Rugby League World Cup: Jack Bostock hat-trick inspires Australia to thrilling 24-22 victory over New Zealand in opener
articles.summary: Pool A game between Australia and New Zealand opened Rugby League World Cup in front of a sold out Sydney crowd; the 24-22 win for the Kangaroos puts them top of Pool A; England get their campaign under way against Tonga on Saturday
articles.body:
It was a breath-taking match that could go down as one of the greatest clashes between the two nations, with Jack Bostock's hat-trick proving decisive despite the Kiwis dominating for much of the contest.

The thrilling showdown drew the biggest crowd for a Test match in 50 years, surpassing the previous benchmark set in 1974.

The result gives defending champions Australia the perfect start to their campaign, sending them straight to the top of Pool A.

The sides were locked at 10-10 at half-time after an enthralling opening 40 minutes.

New Zealand crossed through a Casey McLean try, converted by Jamayne Isaako, who also added two penalties to keep the Kiwis firmly in contention.

However, Australia hit back with two breakaway tries, as Bostock and Tom Trbojevic both raced over, with Reece Walsh adding the conversion to the latter's score.

The Kangaroos were forced to navigate a spell without Kotoni Staggs, who was sent to the sin bin for impeding Kodi Nikorima as he chased a kick with a try-scoring opportunity in sight.

The second half saw Kalyn Ponga produce moments of brilliance for the Kiwis, crossing for two tries before being forced off with an arm injury - but Australia refused to buckle.

Walsh produced a brilliant burst of pace to race away for a try, before debutant Bostock rose highest on two occasions to complete his hat-trick.

It proved just enough for the Kangaroos to hold on and secure a thrilling two-point victory.

Kangaroos and Kiwis provide contest to remember

With an incredible atmosphere at the Allianz Stadium, international rugby league took centre stage and once the National Anthems and Haka were complete, the players did all the talking.

The Kiwis were on top from very early in the game and turned that into points through a stunning McLean effort in the corner. Ronaldo Mulitalo jumped highest to send out the pass for the centre's gravity-defying finish. With Isaako's conversion, New Zealand had a quick 6-0 lead.

Despite such dominance, Australia took their moments. The first came on the 20th minute when young Bostock intercepted Jerome Hughes' pass and raced all the way downfield to score on his debut to bring the Kangaroos within two points.

The first of Isaako's penalties then followed as star man Walsh sent a goal-line dropout attempt straight into touch. New Zealand led 8-4.

Just six minutes later, Australia pulled off a carbon copy of their opening try but on the other side of the field. This time, winger Trbejovic came up with the interception and used his pace to go the length of the field. Walsh converted to reinstate the two-point advantage.

The enthralling first half was not done there.

With just minutes left on the clock, Nikorima chased down the grubber kick in what looked like a try-scoring opportunity but he was impeded by Staggs. While not given as a penalty try, the Australian centre was sent to the sin bin and Isaako obliged with the boot to bring scores level at 10-10 with 40 still to play.

Five minutes into the second half, New Zealand punished that sin bin further, they continuously shifted out to the left and when the massive overlap emerged from a tap and go, Ponga had all the space to go over for his first try and with Isaako's conversion, they led 16-10.

A huge error from Trbejovic was the next big moment of the game and New Zealand thought Mulitalo had scored off the back of it as he knocked on and the Kiwis went over through Mulitalo. However, Isaiah Papali'i was judged offside in the build-up.

That saw the momentum swing and just a set later, Bostock jumped highest in the corner to go over for his second in a stunning display of athleticism. Walsh converted and with just over 20 minutes remaining, the scores were level once again.

While that swing could have had New Zealand on the back foot, some more Ponga brilliance saw them take a 22-16 lead. He sliced through the defensive line, put on an audacious step past Walsh, and dived over despite his shorts being pulled halfway down for half of his run.

Just as one exhilarating player made his mark, it was then the turn of the other fullback in Walsh. On around halfway, he came up with a right footstep to gallop away to the corner.

In more drama, Walsh, who had been goal kicking throughout the match, could not complete the conversion after being sick on the sideline. That meant Latrell Mitchell had to step up but sent it just wide.

With Ponga forced from the field with what looked like an arm injury, New Zealand had 10 minutes left to try and pull off an almighty win. Australia would not give up, though, and in the 76th minute, Bostock climbed highest once again to complete his hat-trick and give his country the lead.

Walsh, back on kicking duties, could not convert but that did not matter as Australia scrambled hard for the final few minutes to secure a statement win.

Australia have been world champions since the 2013 Rugby League World Cup and look like they are on the path to try and make it four World Cups in a row.

Bostock: Everything I've ever dreamed of

Australia debutant and hat-trick hero, Jack Bostock:

"I can't put it into words. That was everything I've ever dreamed of putting this green and gold jersey on.

"Munster has done it so many times in World Cups and he kicked it really well - so I thought I may as well come down with it!"

New Zealand captain James Fisher-Harris:

"That's Test footy. For the full 80 we were battling. Much respect to Australia - a few moments went their way.

articles.title: Immanuel Feyi-Waboso expected to be fit for England's Nations Championship fixture against Australia in November
articles.summary: Immanuel Feyi-Waboso tweaked hamstring playing for Exeter against Newcastle; wing is on track to feature in England’s opening Nations Championship Test against Australia on November 8; England then play Japan on November 14 and New Zealand on November 21
articles.body:
The explosive wing hobbled off in the second half of Exeter's 34-28 victory over Newcastle last weekend.

Chiefs director of rugby Rob Baxter insists Feyi-Waboso is expected to return sooner rather than later, suggesting he should be available for the opening Nations Championship fixture against Australia on November 8.

Baxter said: "Manny's got some awareness there. The scan doesn't show up too much and on testing he's very good.

"We're hopeful that we can treat the symptoms he's showing and see where he gets to over the next week or so.

"Looking at how he's reporting post-game and (Monday), there's nothing I'm hearing from our physios saying there should be a long-term issue now.

"Seeing that he's reporting so well and he's functionally so good, there may not need to be too much intervention."

Feyi-Waboso has been limited to 16 caps since making his debut two years ago due to a series of injuries including shoulder, hamstring and concussion.

The 23-year-old is one of 25 centrally-contracted players, giving England control over his medical arrangements, and he has already been assessed by one of their physios.

Baxter added: "England like players to go and see certain specialists and we're in a delicate time for both parties.

"We're desperate for Manny to play because we've got some important games and England want him to be able to feature in the autumn.

"Hopefully there won't be any dispute based on where Manny feels he is."

articles.title: Rugby League World Cup 2026: Kallum Watkins replaces injured Morgan Smithies in England squad
articles.summary: Kallum Watkins is called up as a late replacement to England's Rugby League World Cup squad after Morgan Smithies is forced to withdraw through injury.
articles.body:
Kallum Watkins has been called up to England's Rugby League World Cup squad as a late replacement after Morgan Smithies was forced to withdraw through injury.

The 35-year-old Leeds Rhinos second-row forward is set to take part in his fourth World Cup having previously featured in 2013, 2017 and 2022.

The loss of lock and second-row forward Smithies, who is set to join Perth Bears for the 2027 NRL season, comes as a blow to England.

However, in Watkins, head coach Brian McDermott has found a replacement he knows well having previously coached him during a trophy-laden spell at Leeds.

"It's really unfortunate what has happened to Morgan with an injury picked up in training," said McDermott.

"Morgan has been great since we entered camp. He's a real team player and his work ethic and toughness are qualities that we will certainly miss.

"Kallum enjoyed a terrific season with Leeds this year and has been part of our England performance programme building into this World Cup.

"I look forward to welcoming him into camp as we step up our preparations."

Watkins, who has 32 caps, is set to arrive in Perth before England's World Cup opener against Tonga on Saturday (10:05 BST) but will not play.

He started his career as a centre before shifting into the pack in recent years and will be available for England's other group matches against France and Papua New Guinea.

articles.title: Rugby League World Cup: England rocked by injury with Perth Bears-bound Morgan Smithies ruled out
articles.summary: Morgan Smithies has been ruled out of the Rugby League World Cup in a blow to England head coach Brian McDermott; he has been replaced by Leeds Rhinos' Kallum Watkins
articles.body:
Leeds Rhinos' Kallum Watkins is set to depart for Australia to take the place of lock and second-row forward Smithies.

Watkins, who played in two of last year's three Ashes Tests against Australia, will arrive in Perth ahead of the weekend but is not set to feature in Saturday's opener against Tonga.

Head coach Brian McDermott said: "It's really unfortunate what has happened to Morgan with an injury picked up in training.

"Morgan has been great since we entered camp. He's a real team player and his work ethic and toughness are qualities that we will certainly miss.

"Kallum enjoyed a terrific season with Leeds this year and has been part of our England Performance Programme building into this World Cup.

"I look forward to welcoming him into camp as we step up our preparations."

Watkins, 35, started out his glittering career as a centre but has transitioned to the pack in recent years and has played under McDermott at club level during his first stint as a player at Headingley.

Should he feature, he will play in his fourth Rugby League World Cup after previously representing his country on home soil in 2013 and 2022 plus Down Under when England progressed to the 2017 final.

articles.title: Ben Thomas: Cardiff centre to miss start of Nations Championship for Wales
articles.summary: Centre Ben Thomas is set to miss the opening games of the Nations Championship but Taulupe Faletau is expected to play before November.
articles.body:
Wales centre Ben Thomas is set to miss the start of the Nations Championship but Cardiff team-mate Taulupe Faletau is expected to feature before the tournament returns in November.

Wales head coach Steve Tandy names his autumn squad next week, with the opening match against Japan on 7 November at the Principality Stadium followed by further home matches against New Zealand and Australia.

Thomas, who started at inside centre for Wales' 43-0 defeat to South Africa in Durban back in July, is sidelined with a calf injury.

"He'll be able to definitely form part of the Nations Championship, but might not recover for the first or second game," said Cardiff head coach Corniel van Zyl.

Thomas, 27, has played 19 internationals for Wales and shared the number 12 role with Joe Hawkins in 2026 for Tandy's team.

Eddie James has been regularly selected at outside centre for Wales but is an option at inside centre.

Listen: Scrum V with the Welsh Tigers at Leicester

Fight for Wales spots heats up as under-threat regions win

Dragons suffer Woodman bicep injury blow

Whether Faletau proves his fitness remains to be seen after another false start before Cardiff's 29-5 United Rugby Championship (URC) defeat against Leinster in Dublin last Saturday.

Faletau was named in their starting line-up on Thursday afternoon, although van Zyl admitted the Wales number eight still had a few boxes to tick because of niggles.

Cardiff made the call not to field the 35-year-old for the first time since a shoulder injury suffered at Sharks in March just before kick-off on Saturday.

"He was probably just a little bit uncomfortable in himself and the way he felt about his readiness to play the game," said van Zyl.

"That's always what we say about players being honest and that's the way I want to approach everything.

"There are no major concerns in terms of long-term injuries or not being available potentially this week."

When asked whether he will play in the next couple of weeks, van Zyl replied: "I believe so, 100%, That's definitely the plan."

Whether that is enough for Tandy to consider the three times British and Irish Lions tourist remains to be seen.

Before Wales meet up, Cardiff have two games, with an away trip to play Northampton on Sunday in Europe's Champions Cup opener before hosting Sharks five days later in the URC.

In-form Taine Basham was a last-minute replacement for Faletau, having travelled to Dublin as a precaution, and continued his strong start to the season as his side's most dynamic carrier.

"I have to take my hat off for Taine because it was less than a minute to kick-off and then all of a sudden he had to strap his legs and put his mouth guard in," said van Zyl.

"It was pleasing to see how he reacted to that situation and he performed really well, so credit to his character."

Basham, 26, won the last of his 17 Wales caps against England in the 2024 Six Nations.

He is the form number eight in Welsh domestic rugby and faces a battle for selection in the competitive back-row area.

Van Zyl believes Wales will consider Basham's credentials.

"If you look at the back end of last season, where he came into his own and this season's form, I've got no doubt they will definitely look at him," said van Zyl.

articles.title: England's Red Roses: John Mitchell makes four changes to starting XV for Canada WXV Global Series Test in Toronto
articles.summary: John Mitchell makes four changes to Red Roses side to face Canada in Toronto; Amy Cokayne, Tatyana Heard, Hannah Botterman, Abi Burton in; Watch Australia vs New Zealand in Bledisloe Cup Test on Saturday live on Sky Sports Main Event from 6am
articles.body:
Experienced hooker Amy Cokayne, centre Tatyana Heard, loosehead prop Hannah Botterman and back-row Abi Burton are each brought in to start in Toronto by head coach John Mitchell.

The Red Roses face Canada on Saturday a month after t hey were held to an entertaining 26-26 draw in Exeter , and having most-recently needed a try in the final play of the match to beat New Zealand at Allianz Stadium, Twickenham.

To make way for the four alterations, centre Helena Rowland, hooker Bryony Field and prop Mackenzie Carson drop down to the replacements bench, while flanker Sadia Kabeya returns to the bench following a leg injury with Marlie Packer missing England's North American tour ahead of partner Rosie Galligan giving birth.

Bristol Bears forward Demelza Short (20) features as a replacement for the first time in the WXV Global Series.

The second Test will take place in front of a record crowd for a standalone women's rugby match in North America.

"The first Test in Exeter gave us a valuable opportunity to test our game under pressure and identify where we can improve," head coach John Mitchell said. "As we continue to build towards 2029, our focus is on raising our level, strengthening our connections and continuing to evolve as a team. "Playing in Toronto presents a different environment and challenge, and we're excited by the opportunity to express our game, improve our performance and continue to grow as the Red Roses. We're looking forward to the challenge of the second Test."

articles.title: Red Roses: Amy Cokayne back as England prepare to face Canada
articles.summary: England welcome back the experience of Amy Cokayne at hooker as their 41-match unbeaten run comes under serious threat away to Canada.
articles.body:
England welcome back the experienced Amy Cokayne at hooker as their 41-match unbeaten run goes on the line against Rugby World Cup runners-up Canada in Toronto on Friday.

Cokayne has not played Test rugby since scoring the Red Roses' final try in a Grand Slam-sealing win over France in Bordeaux in May.

Saracens' Bryony Field, who has three caps to Cokayne's 94, drops to the bench after deputising impressively in the first half of the WXV Global Series last month.

During that part of the campaign, Canada ended England's near four-year winning streak with a nail-biting 26-26 draw at Sandy Park in Exeter.

Live on the BBC iPlayer, BBC Sport website and app

Coach Kevin Rouet has targeted victory over the Red Roses as the main aim for Canada in 2026, with his team playing on home soil for the first time in more than 14 months.

Canada also play England in Ottawa on Friday, 23 October, with the two matches branded as the hosts' Rugby Rematch Tour.

The attendance for the Toronto match is expected to exceed 14,000, comfortably beating the previous record for a standalone women's rugby match in North America which was set when 11,453 watched Canada beat the United States in the most recent home match.

Elsewhere in England's line-up, prop Hannah Botterman features after coming on as a replacement in the dramatic win over New Zealand last time out.

With Marlie Packer staying in England as her partner and Red Roses team-mate Rosie Galligan is due to give birth, Abi Burton takes a spot in the back row, while Tatyana Heard's direct running is preferred to Helena Rowland's playmaking ability at inside centre.

Sadia Kabeya, who missed the win over the Black Ferns with a leg injury, is on the bench, alongside Bristol Bears' 20-year-old Demelza Short, who covers second row.

"The first Test in Exeter gave us a valuable opportunity to test our game under pressure and identify where we can improve," England head coach John Mitchell said.

"Playing in Toronto presents a different environment and challenge, and we're excited by the opportunity to express our game, improve our performance and continue to grow as the Red Roses."

articles.title: Aaron Wainwright, Olly Cracknell and Tommy Reffell: Wales back-row trio starring for Leicester in the Prem
articles.summary: Aaron Wainwright, Olly Cracknell and Tommy Reffell have starred in Leicester Tigers' encouraging start to the season.
articles.body:
Wainwright, Cracknell and Reffell. Not an accountancy firm, even if it sounds like one, but the trio of Welsh back-rowers whose numbers are stacking up at Leicester this season.

To give them their full names, Aaron Wainwright, Olly Cracknell and Tommy Reffell have starred in Tigers' encouraging start to the Prem campaign.

The trio had never played together before but have started all three of Leicester's league games, with victories against Newcastle and Gloucester, and a narrow defeat to Saracens.

Wainwright and Reffell have been employed as flankers with Cracknell at number eight.

"I think we've complemented each other well and gone and out gone about our business, so it's been enjoyable to get stuck in," Wainwright told the Scrum V podcast.

They form a well-rounded trio with Wainwright and Cracknell providing the ball-carrying grunt and defensive power, and Reffell proving the master poacher.

"Both Crackers and Waino are physical, dynamic players, but their knowledge of the game is also excellent, being at the right place at the right time," said Reffell.

"They know when to carry, so seeing them do that in the Premiership has been great."

The three players have arrived at Welford Road at contrasting times during their careers.

Wainwright is the new kid on the block despite, having played 70 internationals in a nine-year Wales career that includes a Grand Slam title and two Six Nations triumphs. He has also played at two World Cups.

Wainwright moved to Leicester after almost a decade at Dragons to join a growing influx of Wales' top players in England.

Wales captains Dewi Lake and Jac Morgan have joined Gloucester, with Louis Rees-Zammit, Dafydd Jenkins, Tomos Williams, Nicky Smith, Rhys Carre, Archie Griffin, Tomas Francis and Christ Tshiunza among those also playing in the Prem.

Wainwright is in a lift-share with Reffell and fly-half Billy Searle.

"Reff is keeping keeping me company in the morning, so he's doing a good job of helping me settle in," said Wainwright.

"He has helped introduce me to everyone and it felt a bit like it was a first day at school.

"I was nervous but everyone's been welcoming and I feel I have settled in."

Wainwright made an instant impression with his team-mates on his debut after setting up Wales wing Gabriel Hamer-Webb with a try-scoring pass against Saracens.

"He moves like a back and hits like a forward," said Hamer-Webb.

"He has this engine on him that just does not stop and that's part of the Leicester Tigers DNA.

"He's also got that soft touch that you saw when he assisted me against Saracens with that great pass.

"I have seen him play before but to be on the same pitch as him and see how he moves, he is phenomenal."

Wainwright has also become a firm fans' favourite, as indicated by an incident after the away victory at Newcastle.

"I saw some of the fans and there's a few that had the headbands and wigs on and I had a photo," said Wainwright.

"One of them just snuck me a packet of Welsh cakes to take home on the bus. That was a nice touch."

The 29-year-old still has a fondness for his home city having opened a cafe in Newport.

He has also taken on a director of coaching role at his boyhood club Whiteheads RFC, despite living in a Leicestershire village almost three hours away.

Wainwright deserved his move after being such a loyal servant , playing in a Dragons side that was not used to winning. There were 33 victories, 97 defeats and eight draws in his 138 matches.

Leicester are preparing for the start of the Champions Cup matches away in Pau on Sunday, with Wainwright having never played in the top-tier competition.

He missed the only two Champions Cup games that Dragons played while he was at Rodney Parade, which came back in 2020.

Now, one of Wales' elite back rowers is finally set to grace Europe's elite tournament.

Cracknell recalls first cap as he hopes for Wales recall

Wainwright and flanker Morgan are currently certainties for Steve Tandy's Wales Nations Championship squad to be announced on 20 October, with the pair likely to fill two of the three starting spots.

Reffell and Cracknell are playing well enough to be included but there is stiff competition. Both Leicester players have experienced the disappointment this year of being left out of Wales squads.

Five out of the six starting back-rowers in the Leicester and Gloucester league match last Friday were Welsh, with Morgan and Freddie Thomas part of the Cherry and Whites trio.

Tandy can also call on Cardiff trio Alex Mann, James Botham and Taine Basham, with veteran Taulupe Faletau close to a return from injury.

Throw in Scarlets duo Taine Plumtree and Josh Macleod and Exeter's Kane James and you see the wealth of options available.

Cracknell featured in the 2026 Six Nations but was not included in the summer squad.

While he is hoping for an international recall, Cracknell will never forget his first cap, earned eight years after originally being named in a Wales squad.

Warren Gatland called up the forward - born in Leeds with a Welsh grandfather - for the 2017 Six Nations but he was not given his debut.

Cracknell left Ospreys for London Irish in 2021 and their demise led to a move to Leicester the following summer.

After impressing for Tigers, he was recalled by Tandy, who was his first Ospreys coach.

Cracknell was 31 when he made his debut as a replacement in the 52-28 defeat by Argentina in November 2025.

"It was such a long journey," said Cracknell. "I wasn't born in Wales, but I signed up for the Exiles programme when I was 16.

"I was always proud of that side and I moved to north Wales when I was 19.

"I played for Wales Under-20s and went to the World Cup in New Zealand.

"I was involved in the Six Nations squad in 2017 but did not play.

"When it came back around with Tandy, who gave me my first professional contract, it was a full circle moment and probably my proudest achievement.

"There was a time where I didn't think I'd get another rugby contract, so to get back and have that first game was an experience I never thought I'd have."

One-club stalwart Reffell starts season in style

While Wainwright and Cracknell both joined Leicester after starting their careers elsewhere, Reffell is a one-club man. He joined the Welford Road academy aged 15 and made his senior debut at 17.

He is a Leicester stalwart who is regarded as one of the league's best foraging flankers, and has started the season in excellent fashion.

Reffell was player of the match in the Newcastle victory, and enjoyed a battle royale with Morgan last weekend in the duel of Wales' premier openside flankers.

So much so, Wales and British and Irish Lions legend Sam Warburton could not separate them in commentary, saying the Welsh starting back-row should be Morgan, Reffell and Wainwright.

Tandy left Reffell out of two Wales squads in the 2025-26 season and did not even include him when Morgan was ruled out through injury.

Reffell, 27, returned for the summer series and made an appearance from the replacements' bench against South Africa in the 43-0 defeat - but his experience ensures he takes nothing for granted.

"As a professional rugby player, you never want to accept those decisions," said the flanker from Pencoed, who captained Leicester in last season's Prem Cup final win against Exeter.

"You always want to keep pushing yourself to get better. All you can control is yourself and what you do. There's no point complaining and worrying about it.

"It's about getting yourself in the right space of mind and place to continue banging on the door and hopefully get your shot to get back in there."

Whether there are one, two or three Leicester back-rowers in Tandy's autumn squad remains to be seen - but Tigers fans will simply be looking for more of the same this season.

articles.title: Papua New Guinea: How the Kumuls, and now Orchids, inspire hope for a nation
articles.summary: World Cup co-hosts Papua New Guinea's love of rugby league manifests itself in the Kumuls and the Orchids national teams, two badges of hope and unity for the island.
articles.body:
"Back home when we play in front of our own fans, just to see the fans, the crowd get behind us, singing the national anthem... it makes me cry every time."

Edwin Ipape gets emotional when travelling with his Papua New Guinea team-mates to the national stadium.

Children, so mad about rugby league that they will fashion a ball out of anything they can find, run alongside the team bus, eager to catch a glimpse of their heroes. Players are mobbed wherever they go.

The buzz around rugby league in Papua New Guinea can sometimes be daunting for visiting teams. In the past, passion has boiled over to the point where police have fired tear gas into the crowds.

But the national game – and in particular its men's national team, the Kumuls – is also a powerful symbol of unity in a land that can be torn apart by tribal fighting and where more than 800 different languages and dialects are spoken.

When the PNG fans are at their best and noisiest, a 15,000 crowd can sound like twice that number and is so loud that the players on the field cannot hear each other.

They will be at full volume this month when the island's capital Port Moresby is the venue for four Rugby League World Cup matches, as PNG co-hosts the tournament with Australia and New Zealand.

"People in Papua New Guinea probably don't know who the prime minister is, but they know all the NRL [National Rugby League] players," joked Elsie Albert, a prop who plays for PNG's women's side – the Orchids – and for Parramatta Eels in Australia's NRL Women's Premiership.

So, how has an island perched off Australia's northern tip become so obsessed with the sport?

Australia, Papua New Guinea, New Zealand

Listen to live commentary on every men's match, and key women's matches - with coverage on BBC Radio 5 Live, BBC Radio 5 Sports Extra, BBC Sounds and the BBC Sport website and app

The seeds were sown by Australian miners in the 1930s, who introduced the game, one with deep roots in New South Wales and Queensland, to the local population.

It took hold as the devotion spread. The ferocious physicality of rugby league sat easily with the Papuans, who had long fought battles without a ball on their soil.

These days, the people of PNG are among the most knowledgeable and passionate. Only the Cook Islands can lay similar claims to an all-out obsession with the game in terms of national importance.

Sometimes that fervour spills over, with violence souring matches in their domestic league, , external something the authorities are keen to stamp out. In the past, tear gas was needed to quell over-excited crowds, such as when Great Britain came to tour in the early 1990s.

Generally though, rugby league is more of a peacekeeper. Villages will settle around a television set to watch rugby league, whether it is the NRL or Super League.

Participation levels are high. There are thousands of would-be Edwin Ipapes across the island, running about on bits of grass, on gravel, on the scrawniest patch of clear land somewhere, anywhere they can get the ball out and play.

The games can be rough, bordering on brutal. They are the perfect breeding ground for talent. But kit can be basic.

"If you're lucky enough, you play with a rugby league ball," Ipape recalled of his childhood, growing up in Mount Hagen, in the Highlands of Papua New Guinea.

"Otherwise, you play with containers, you put stuff in it, fill it up and then make it like a ball and whatever... whatever we can get our hands on, we may pretend that it was our rugby ball.

"I remember saving up my lunch money to buy myself one of those American footballs and using it as a rugby ball so we could play."

The Highlands of Papua New Guinea were a testing place to grow up - there is a long history of brutal tribal rivalries. Today, violence in those parts of the country has escalated - as access to increasingly sophisticated weaponry has brought deadly consequences.

Ipape, though, only ever had eyes for rugby league. Larsen Marape and Menzie Yere were the heroes of his youth: the faces on the posters adorning his walls in Mount Hagen.

The sport not only brings unity to the country - for those who make it to the top, it also offers a chance to cross the globe.

Ipape, 27, has played for his country, and travelled worldwide. The hooker now plays in Super League for Leigh Leopards.

The 'Birds of Paradise' - as Kumuls translates - have been life-transforming.

"Rugby league has given me pretty much everything," he said. "It's instilled discipline and it's taught me a lot of lessons about life.

"I've welled up with tears a few times on our way to the stadium in Papua New Guinea, just looking at the young kids running alongside the bus.

"I'm so blessed and privileged to be in the position to represent my country. It's a dream I'm living right now."

For any young hopeful looking to become the next Ipape, the first goal is to play for a village, then a province. Then it is the PNG Hunters, who play in Australia's Queensland Cup.

That can be the ticket to the big leagues, whether that be the NRL - as it was for former Melbourne Storm centre Justin Olam - or Super League, as it has been for Ipape.

From 2028 onwards, there will be an NRL team based on the island, the PNG Chiefs.

While much of their initial recruitment has been high-profile, such as Samoa half-back Jarome Luai, compatriot Brian To'o, and New Zealand international Joey Manu, Papuan players have also been sought to bolster the ranks.

Visiting teams can sometimes find the excitement around rugby league in Papua New Guinea unsettling. Any familiar face from the sport draws attention - but the fans only want to show affection and respect.

"We went to a little market and people were recognising us," Leigh Leopards' Papuan hooker Liam Horne told BBC Sport. "We actually needed a lift to go to one of these shopping centres, so we just hitchhiked.

"We got this random guy to pick us up and he couldn't believe it. He had two Kumuls in his back seat and he was freaking out.

"The people over there, they love it. They're welcoming."

Some of the Kumuls of today are second-generation Papuans born and raised in Australia, such as Leigh back-rower Jacob Alick-Weincke.

Being a PNG international is a chance to connect with the culture, understand more about their heritage, upbringing, and the people.

"People there just want to be around you in your presence," Alick-Weincke added.

"We always go to the shops or go to local villages. We went to one of the markets last time we were over there. That was a really cool experience. Just people everywhere."

The rise of the women's team - chronicled in the 2019 documentary Power Meri, , external which followed the Orchids to their debut World Cup in 2017 - has been helped by Elsie Albert's star power.

Albert is PNG's first female superstar - but that meant challenging some old values back home.

"Women were supposed to stay at home and do household chores, so when this great game came over [for women], it was seen as a threat to the culture," Albert said in 2023 as part of an NRL storytelling campaign.

"The pioneering girls had men throwing bottles at them into the stadium, but in 2019 everything changed for us when we played England."

In that two-Test series, England won the first match 24-10 in Goroka. But the second, in Port Moresby, brought a memorable - and defining - 20-16 victory for the hosts.

"You could feel the atmosphere," Albert recalled. "The crowd was there and to get a win in front of everyone, especially the men... for them to see that women could do what men can do, was a great feeling.

"You could feel it was going to change. Rugby league is a great way for us to to advocate for change."

Even well-known rugby league family names of the past are growing new branches, with Fleur Ginn Wagambie following in the footsteps of elders John and Richard when she made her PNG debut in 2025 - and now hopes to make a World Cup debut.

"I've always wanted to represent the Orchids and I was really lucky last year to make my debut in the Pacific Cup," Wagambie, a Parramatta team-mate of Albert, told ABC Pacific.

"Being lucky enough to play in a World Cup, in Port Moresby, in front of my family is really exciting."

Papua New Guinea's rugby league influence can be felt at Championship club London Broncos.

Jason Demetriou, the Kumuls head coach, is in charge at Plough Lane, and his influence persuaded a host of Papuan players to come over.

Championship player of the year Gairo Voro, full-back Morea Morea, prop Epil Kapinias, centres Alex Max and Robert Mathias, hooker Finley Glare and back-rower Jeremiah Simbiken were all recruited by the Super League aspirant Broncos.

Together, they steered the club to a treble - the Championship League Leaders' Shield, the 1895 Cup and the divisional Grand Final title.

Their progress alerted the PNG Chiefs, who have signed Voro, Glare and Morea for the 2028 season onwards.

"There's going to be eyeballs on every player in the World Cup," Demetriou added.

"We're playing against Lebanon, which will be stacked full of NRL players, playing against England that are full of Super League and NRL players, and Samoa, which is one of the top international sides in the world at the moment.

"We know what's in front of us, but on the flip side of that, they're going to play against PNG as well. We have to make sure that when they go out on the field, they understand that there's some elite level players out there.

"If we want opportunities, we want to be respected, then we need to start with beating teams on the world stage."

Santos National Football Stadium - where the co-hosts will play the four Rugby League World Cup matches they are staging - has a capacity of just under 15,000. It will seem a lot more than that on Saturday, though, when the Orchids face France and the Kumuls take on Lebanon. And that will be thanks to the atmosphere.

"Loud" was how Horne put it. "It sounds like 30,000." Kumuls stalwart Lachlan Lam - forced to miss this World Cup because he needs wrist surgery - likened the atmosphere to "a proper scream".

Team-mate Alick-Wiencke said: "I've not experienced anything like it. You can't hear yourself talking to other team-mates and things like that.

"And, just the heat - you can't believe the whole stadium is packed out. It's like 40C and they're up there singing and dancing and carrying on. So the atmosphere is unbelievable."

Whatever happens at this World Cup, rugby league shows no signs of losing its appeal in Papua New Guinea. And the passion of those supporters might yet give Ipape reason to shed a few more tears.

articles.title: New Zealand vs Australia: Les Kiss vows Wallabies will 'return fire' vs All Blacks in Bledisloe Cup Test | Dave Rennie: Quality was coming
articles.summary: Read thoughts of Australia head coach Les Kiss and All Blacks' Dave Rennie ahead of sides meeting in Sydney in return Test and after last week's heavy New Zealand win; watch All Blacks face Australia in Sydney on Saturday October 17 (6am) live on Sky Sports Main Event
articles.body:
Last week, Australia's six-Test unbeaten run came to a shuddering halt when New Zealand ensured they will retain the Bledisloe Cup for a 24th year after powering to a 50-19 victory over the Wallabies at Eden Park.

A competitive first half, perhaps even edged by Australia, saw the All Blacks three points ahead at the break as the sides traded two tries each.

But the second half proved altogether different, as the All Blacks added five further tries in a display of clear dominance.

"It's like anything. You get a knockback, you find out more about yourself and that's what we'll do. We'll work hard on what we have to do," said Kiss.

"Belief is created and sustained by not just wins and losses, they're created by other things. These boys have a strong culture, a strong belief in themselves and a confidence about what they can do.

"But the lessons are there: if you can't get your strengths going and their strengths grow, it makes it a difficult game.

"We'll go back and we'll work on what we have to and try and turn the dial in the right areas that can go to Sydney and return fire."

⁠Australia face some injury issues and will be without ​key centre Len Ikitau, who ​left Saturday's game in the first half ⁠with a head knock, while Hunter Paisami has been suspended.

Jordan Petaia ⁠is also unavailable due to ​an ankle injury, with Corey Toole ​and Kadin Pritchard joining the camp.

Joseph-Aukuso Sua'ali'i moves from the wing to outside center in place of Ikitau, with Harry Potter returning on the left wing.

Declan Meredith will start at No 10 in place of Ben Donaldson, who sustained a leg injury during the first Test in Auckland.

There are also two changes in the front row where former All Black Aidan Ross will start at loosehead and Josh Nasser, a tryscorer last weekend, is named at hooker.

The uncapped Harry McLaughlin-Phillips has been named on the bench.

"Over the last five Tests, we didn't lose the run of ourselves; the boys always said we've got work to do. It doesn't change now," Kiss said.

"We'll have a good look at that game, like we have, get into the nuts and bolts of what we need to get right. How do we get our strengths into the game? How do we just nullify their strengths, and that's what we look at.

"We need to make sure we do the work that gets that done. It'll be making sure we get the things that we feel that can make a difference, that's for sure.

"Once they got their momentum, it was hard to wrestle back."

Rennie: Quality performance from All Blacks had been coming

For the All Blacks, four players have been ruled ‌out of Saturday's Test in ‌Sydney.

New Zealand will be without hooker Asafo Aumua and back-row Anton Segner after both failed ​their second head-injury assessments (HIAs).

Flanker Ethan ⁠Blackadder has picked ⁠up a calf injury, and wing Leroy Carter has been ‌ruled out due to a high ankle sprain, which he suffered while scoring a ‌try in the second half.

Prop George Bower comes in to start at loosehead, lock Fabian Holland will play next to Scott Barrett in the second row and Josh Moorby is named on the left wing. There are five further changes among the replacements.

"I thought a quality performance was coming, but we're also playing a really good side," said New Zealand head coach Dave Rennie.

"So the arm wrestle in the first half [vs Australia at Eden Park], I thought we probably left a couple of opportunities out there, and then they scored late."

Rennie, who coached the Wallabies for three seasons before being dismissed in favour of the ill-fated return of Eddie Jones in 2023, pinpointed a couple of specific areas he feel turned last week's Test in the All Blacks' favour.

"We did a good job looking after the ball, and we played in the right parts of the field. Created good momentum and pressure and benefited from that.

"We're happy. We talked about a number of areas that needed to be better coming out of South Africa, and we saw good shifts. We're confident in our ability, and we felt in Africa that we just lost key moments.

"We had a really good edge around training, and we were well aware of the importance of winning and also the Bledisloe Cup. So it was nice to nail that."

The All Blacks head coach admitted the 31-point defeat at Eden Park won't define this Wallabies side under Kiss, and he expects a stronger performance in Sydney.

"Yeah, look, it's a tough end for them, but it was nice to catch up with a number of those guys post-game. Oh, they'll be hurting.

"They've had a really good year, and I'm confident they'll bounce back next week. Look, I'm very happy with the mindset and the work ethic brutality, and it was spot on."

articles.title: Champions Cup: How are the Irish provinces shaping up for Europe?
articles.summary: BBC Sport NI assesses how the four Irish provinces are tracking before their European campaigns begin on Saturday.
articles.body:
For the first time since 2018, the Investec Champions Cup begins in October with the road to the final in Lyon starting this weekend.

While autumnal fixtures used to be the norm in Europe's top competition, 2026-27 brings an earlier start date than in recent seasons with Irish provinces having just three league games under their collective belts before continental competition kicks off.

After a slow start to their United Rugby Championship (URC) campaigns, how are the sides shaping up to take on the best of the Prem and Top 14? BBC Sport NI takes a look.

Leinster remain Ireland's leading light and will be among the biggest threats to Bordeaux-Begles' ambitions of a third title in a row.

Last season's beaten finalists, though, have a recent reminder of just how hard it will be to derail the reigning champions, having been torn apart 41-19 in May's decider.

Arguably, Leo Cullen's side enter this campaign with a weaker squad than in recent seasons with the likes of James Lowe, Rieko Ioane, Rabah Slimani and Ciaran Frawley among the key departures over the summer.

Only the latter was replaced in kind through the return of Joey Carbery, although the returning 30-year-old is yet to feature in his second stint because of injury.

The side have won an incredible 31 consecutive games in the Champions Cup pool stage, and can expect to extend that run this season, but know they will be judged only by what they do in the sharp end of a competition they have not won since 2018.

If Cullen's final season at the helm is to end with a long-sought fifth star, it will take some titanic performances in the knock-out stage.

Pool fixtures: Clermont (A), Sale (H), Pau (H), Leicester Tigers (A)

While Leinster are keen to put their last Champions Cup outing behind them, fierce rivals Munster were another to exit last season's competition in bitterly disappointing fashion.

The southern province had their destiny in their own hands going into the final round of pool games but were beaten at home by Castres to drop into the Challenge Cup.

Once the Irish standard-setters in this competition, that result perhaps epitomised the recent campaigns of the two-time winners, whose inconsistency in the pool stages has too often left them with an uphill struggle.

It has been four seasons since they last secured a home knock-out tie, and even that was played at Aviva Stadium in Dublin.

While there was a noteworthy win away to La Rochelle in the last 16 of 2025, bringing springtime European rugby back to Thomond Park should be the aim this year.

A draw that includes an away trip to the reigning champions, and the absence of Jack Crowley for at least the first pool fixtures, complicates matters somewhat, but it should be well within the group to improve upon last year.

Pool fixtures: Racing 92 (H), Bristol (A), Bordeaux-Begles (A), Gloucester (H)

The URC's eighth and final Champions Cup qualifier was dealt the harshest of hands in the draw for the pool stages.

Of the past 11 editions of this competition, eight have been won by teams Connacht will face in Europe between now and the end of January.

While Saracens, Exeter and La Rochelle may not be the forces they were when knocking off a few of those titles, they are all still more than handy outfits and Toulouse are alongside Bordeaux-Begles as the favourites to make it to Lyon for the final.

Stuart Lancaster's side were one of the very best teams in the latter half of last season's URC to book their place in this season's competition, but such stern tests arrive with the westerners yet to hit their straps this time around.

They have won one of their opening three league fixtures with scrum issues and discipline among their chief concerns through the early going.

While few sides relish a visit to Galway, a scalp in this pool would sit alongside previous victories over Toulouse as one of the province's biggest European wins.

Pool fixtures: Saracens (H), Exeter Chiefs (A), Toulouse (H), La Rochelle (A)

After never missing out on top-tier European rugby in their history prior to 2024-25, it is now a fate to befall Ulster in consecutive seasons.

Richie Murphy's side made it all the way to the Challenge Cup final last year, when they were thumped by Montpellier in Bilbao.

That reverse, coupled with their league campaign falling away, ensured a second year in the lesser of European rugby's two competitions.

Paired with familiar URC foes Zebre and Dragons, as well as Top 14 pair Bayonne and Perpignan, Ulster will expect to make a return to the knock-out stages, where they beat Racing 92, Exeter Chiefs and La Rochelle a year ago.

It will be at that stage of the competition, however, when their depth is again tested as they juggle the desired run in Europe with the ambition to return to the URC's play-offs after a two-year absence.

The northern province have the talent to make an impact in this competition but ensuring they are not back here in a year's time - in whatever way they manage it - should be the season's goal.

Pool fixtures: Zebre (A), Bayonne (H), Perpignan (A), Dragons (H)

articles.title: Rugby World Cup 2035: Spain bids to host tournament and use Nou Camp and Bernabeu
articles.summary: Barcelona's Nou Camp, Madrid's Bernabeu and the Mestalla in Valencia are all on a list of possible venues as Spain bids to host the Rugby World Cup in 2035.
articles.body:
Barcelona's Nou Camp, Real Madrid's Bernabeu and the Mestalla in Valencia are all on a list of possible stadiums as Spain bids to host the Rugby World Cup in 2035.

The Spanish Rugby Federation says it aims to deliver the "best World Cup in history", connecting the tournament to 700 million Spanish speakers worldwide.

If Spain's bid is successful, the revamped Nou Camp is in line to host the final, which would be the first time the World Cup showpiece has been held in front of more than 100,000 fans.

Argentina and Japan are also bidding to host the tournament, with World Rugby expected to announce its preferred bidder in the spring or summer of 2027.

Spanish rugby authorities say the tournament in 2035 would capitalise on the Fifa World Cup in 2030, with Spain joint hosts along with Morocco and Portugal.

The Rugby World Cup bid has the support of the Spanish government as well as La Liga, with some of the most iconic stadiums in world football on a list of potential venues.

"We have complete confidence in our organisational capability, our sports infrastructure is at the cutting edge of innovation, and we are convinced that hosting Rugby World Cup 2035 will bring new and unique dimensions of hospitality, collaboration, unity and friendship to the global rugby family," said Juan Carlos Martin 'Hansen', executive president of the Spanish federation.

Spain have qualified for the 2027 tournament in Australia, which will be their first appearance at a men's World Cup since 1999.

The Spanish federation has an ambition to triple the number of people playing the sport in the country by 2035 and, ultimately, establish Spain as a Tier One rugby nation.

"Rugby is becoming part of our country's identity," added Martin.

"Working together with World Rugby, we can make Rugby World Cup 2035 a turning point in the global growth of the sport, for the benefit of generations to come."

Seven-time participants in the Women's Rugby World Cup, Spain has hosted two European finals weekends - at Bilbao's San Mames in 2018 and 2026 - while the 2016 Top 14 final was held at the Nou Camp in front of 99,124 supporters.

The San Mames is on a list of 14 stadiums submitted to World Rugby, which will be reduced to 9 or 10 if the Spanish bid is successful.

Spain has also staged World Rugby Sevens events, with further editions confirmed in Castile and Leon for 2027 and 2028 respectively.

Site visits and feasibility assessments are due to take place from December, with World Rugby planning to identify its preferred candidate by the late spring or summer of 2027.

A formal announcement is expected during the 2027 tournament in Australia.

Japan and a South American group of nations led by Argentina have announced their bids.

A tournament in Argentina would also include Brazil, Chile and Uruguay and would break ground as the first Rugby World Cup in South America.

Japan hosted a similarly ground-breaking World Cup in 2019 - the first to take place in Asia - which smashed commercial and audience records.

The 2027 and 2029 World Cups are taking place in Australia, with the US hosting in 2031 and 2033.

Argentina make pitch to host 2035 Rugby World Cup

Spain is a sleeping giant of European rugby, with the sporting culture and infrastructure to become an elite rugby nation.

A World Cup in 2035 would supercharge this ambition, and the prospect of some of the most iconic football stadiums in the world hosting matches is tantalising.

With the World Cups in 2027 and 2031 taking place in Australia and the US, it is also very possible that World Rugby would want to return the tournament to Europe in 2035.

However, Argentina's bid tugs on the heart strings given the magnificent role the Pumas have played in so many World Cups over the decades.

But, while a South American tournament could be wonderful, Argentina and the co-hosts would need to prove to World Rugby they have the infrastructure and financial clout of Spain and Japan.

As was the case with Ireland and South Africa in 2023, the romantic bid is often overlooked in favour of commercial imperatives. This is where Japan come into it as another serious contender, given the huge success on and off the field in 2019.

articles.title: Rugby League World Cup 2026: Australia edge New Zealand in opener
articles.summary: Jack Bostock scores a hat-trick of tries as Australia fight back to win the opening game of the Rugby League World Cup against New Zealand.
articles.body:
Tries : Bostock 3, Trbojevic, Walsh Goals : Walsh 2

Tries : McLean, Ponga 2 Goals : Isaako 3 Penalties : Isaako 2

Opening games of World Cups can often be cautious and reserved non-events. Someone forgot to tell Australia and New Zealand.

This was as good as this sport gets. As good as any sport gets.

These two old foes traded blows - in every sense - for 80 pulsating minutes in a game of staggering skill, brutal intensity and relentless drama.

New Zealand's formidable pack served up a mauling to Australia's forwards for the majority of this opening match of the 2026 Rugby League World Cup but the defending champions did what champions do and somehow chiselled out a victory.

This was scintillating international rugby league, with more than 40,000 fans - the biggest Test match crowd in Sydney for 50 years - witnessing the ultimate smash-and-grab victory by Kevin Walters' side.

Casey McLean's stunning early try gave New Zealand the impetus and they were on top until the final five minutes, when Jack Bostock marked a stunning Kangaroos debut with his third try to decide an epic match.

The Kangaroos were 6-0, 16-10 and 22-16 down - with the Kiwis pounding their line to go another score ahead - but late tries from Reece Walsh and then Bostock turned the match around.

Bostock's dream debut - which included one interception try and two by winning aerial battles to claim spiralling Cameron Munster kicks - was one of many fascinating sub plots.

Kalyn Ponga's match-up against his Australia counterpart Walsh, arguably the sport's biggest star, was another.

The Kiwi full-back scored twice and looked to be coming out on top in their personal battle until Walsh conjured up a superb long-range try to lay the platform for the Kangaroos' last-gasp triumph.

Ponga making his first appearance for New Zealand left the field injured with a suspected broken arm prior to Munster and Bostock reprising their up-and-under show with less than five minutes on the clock and had his left arm in a sling at full time.

Quite how new Queensland coach Darius Boyd selects between the star duo at Origin level next year is anyone's guess. How do you separate arguably the two best full-backs in the game?

While Walsh's superb tackle on Ponga prevented a try in the first-half, the Newcastle Knights man replied by dancing past his Australia counterpart on his way to the second of his tries.

But back came Walsh, delivering a stunning attacking riposte of his own eight minutes later to bring Australia to within two points at 20-22.

Ponga had been the beneficiary of New Zealand's powerhouse pack getting on the front foot for the majority of the match.

As a result, the dash and swagger exhibited by Australia in their Ashes triumph of 12 months ago was largely replaced through necessity by a staunch defence of their line.

Yet somehow, largely thanks to two errant New Zealand passes that allowed Bostock and Tom Trbojevic to race unopposed from distance to score - they were level at 10-10 at the break having been comprehensively outplayed.

When Trobojevic scored, only 18% of the game was played in New Zealand territory.

The second half followed a similar script and as a result this will be a result New Zealand will find hard to stomach.

It was a game for the ages and while England and other side will hope to have their say, many will expect Australia will have to repeat this performance against New Zealand in the final on 15 November if they are to lift the trophy for a 13th time.

Matt's player of the match - Reece Walsh

There were plenty of candidates for this - hat-trick hero Jack Bostock, Kiwi full-back Kalyn Ponga and his packmen James Fisher-Harris, Moses Leota and Isaiah Papali'i, but if it is down to deciding moments then Reece Walsh had ample fingerprints on the victory.

There was a huge defensive effort on Ponga in the first-half when he guided his fellow full-back to the outside and then monstered him with a ball-and-all tackle.

He then showed the fleetfooted magic in his game with a lightning break to torch the Kiwis and deliver a try that just tipped the balance in the Kangaroos' favour.

Given his recent injury absence, Walsh's calves and lungs were burning at times while a vomiting spout just outlined the lengths he was willing to go to help his team.

Knowing you've got a matchwinner in the ranks helps Australia deal with being under the pump as they were on significant occasions in this, and Walsh delivered.

articles.title: Canada vs England: Hosts expect landmark win over Red Roses says Apps
articles.summary: Scrum-half Olivia Apps believes the time is right for Canada to end England's four-year unbeaten run when the teams meet on Friday
articles.body:
In Exeter last month, there were two expressions on Olivia Apps' face that bode ill for England.

Apps, Canada's starting scrum-half, aimed it at, and shared it with, England trio Zoe Harrison, Jess Breach and Marlie Packer, who she has played alongside with Saracens in the PWR this season.

"Playing at Saracens has really helped to take the mystique away from all these names that you see on a teamsheet," Apps told BBC Sport.

"You know them as people and it takes away that uncertainty, [the] mysterious part."

In the final play of the game, with the scores level and Canada in possession on their own 22m, Apps was stationed on the wing, waiting for a pass that never came.

Rather than spin and gamble for victory, full-back Claire Gallagher opted to boot the ball into touch and secure a draw.

"It was the right call, but when the message came on [from coach Kevin Rouet] I had to ask three times, because I thought there was no way," says Apps.

"We just thought, obviously we were going to run the ball and try and score."

Rather than joy at becoming the first team to avoid defeat against England in nearly four years, Apps and her team sagged with disappointment that they hadn't had been able to decisively down rugby's most dominant team.

Familiarity, and scoreboard equity, has bred belief.

Fortunately, Apps has two more shots coming up.

Canada take on England in Toronto on Friday and then, seven days later, again in Ottawa.

The matches are the first time Canada have played on home soil since a Rugby World Cup warm-up match in August 2025.

More than 15,000 Canada fans are expected to pack BMO Field.

The two Tests have been sold to them as the Rugby Rematch Tour, riffing on Canada's defeat by England in the Rugby World Cup final a year ago.

A rematch with a revised outcome has been Rouet's aim for the whole of 2026.

"Being a different squad from the World Cup allows us to have more of a belief in our ability to beat England," says Apps.

"We've been together for five weeks, we have home advantage, mentally we feel really confident. There is definitely more of an expectation now.

"Overall, I think we'd be really, really disappointed in ourselves if we couldn't get a victory this weekend."

Doing so would further fuel the momentum of women's rugby in Canada.

While England benefit from top-class facilities, a deep player pool and central contracts, Canada launched a crowdfunding campaign before the last Rugby World Cup to cover the cost of their training camps.

After Canada's stirring campaign, the country's government announced a new 755m Canadian dollars (£401m) funding package for sport in the country in May. , external

"I think our showing at the World Cup was like a big final push to get that from the government," says Apps.

"We've yet to see what that it means specifically for rugby, but we've heard really positive things."

A behind-the-scenes documentary on Canada's Rugby World Cup campaign, called All Heart, has just been released and, in conjunction with the two Tests against England, should boost Apps and others' profiles.

"England has done a phenomenal job of that," says Apps.

"The way they tell the story of their athletes and how their athletes get so much space and opportunity to showcase who they are and their brand, alongside rugby.

"It's amazing to see where female rugby athletes can go."

Live on the BBC iPlayer, BBC Sport website and app

Apps has seen that close up over the past year. She initially signed with Saracens as short-term injury cover last October, but has been in sensational form, playing a key part in the north London side's first PWR title in four years and being named the top flight's player of the season.

A new three-year contract extension was announced this week.

Saracens invited Sue Schilling, the chief executive of UK Alopecia, a condition that Apps was diagnosed with aged seven, to record a congratulatory message, , external emphasising the importance of Apps as a role model.

The security of Apps' Saracens contract means she knows her path to the Los Angeles Olympics, where she and Canada will defend the silver medals they won in Paris, and the next Rugby World Cup in Australia in 2029.

While she and her fellow Canadians - world player of the year Sophie de Goede, Alysha Corrigan and Julia Omokhuale are among her compatriots at Saracens - have struggled to source pumpkin puree and decent maple syrup in London, they have found the highest level of women's club rugby in the world.

"There is such a strong pool of experience that it does just feel very stimulating and challenging," Apps says.

"Saracens has an environment with a winning culture which really drives performance and competition. It's something which I really enjoy."

Come the final whistle on Friday, England will hope not to see the smile from Apps which would mean the demise of their long unbeaten run.

articles.title: Rugby League World Cup 2026: Reece Walsh vomits and Kalyn Ponga plays through pain
articles.summary: Australia's Reece Walsh exerted himself to the point of throwing up, while New Zealand's Kalyn Ponga tried to play on with a suspected broken arm in a dramatic Men's Rugby League World Cup opener.
articles.body:
If anyone doubted the physical commitment of rugby league's greatest stars, they only needed to watch an exhausted Reece Walsh doubled up and vomiting during Thursday's epic World Cup opener between Australia and New Zealand.

And during the Kangaroos' dramatic 24-22 victory in Sydney, there were plenty of other examples of that commitment - aside from the normal rough and tumble this punishing sport regularly delivers.

New Zealand full-back Kalyn Ponga bravely battled on for 20 minutes with a suspected broken arm before almost having to be scraped off the pitch minutes before hat-trick hero Jack Bostock's winning try for the Kangaroos.

Mitchell Moses initially tried to run off a calf issue before being forced from the field just after the break, while Australia captain Isaah Yeo demonstrated his durability against a powerhouse Kiwis pack, having elected to delay surgery on his injured pectoral muscle just in order play in the tournament.

But understandably, much of the focus was on the star full-backs - Ponga and Walsh.

The Kangaroos number one was playing for the first time for eight weeks after recovering from an ankle injury.

And he delivered a superb try-saving tackle on Ponga during the first-half before scoring a with a sensational 60-metre burst to lay the platform for the Kangaroos' last-gasp victory.

"Walshy was very good tonight having not played for eight weeks," said Australia head coach Kevin Walters.

"I thought he was really good. That try-saving tackle he did is equal to anything that he can do an attack, and then he comes up with a couple of big plays in attack as well.

"He's cramping and vomiting and all sorts of things. He didn't have the energy to kick the goal. He's a chucker [he throws up]. People get nicknames and his nickname is 'Chucker'.

"He's not an endurance athlete. He's a power athlete and he had some big efforts there a couple of times, back-to-back and we've seen him do that before."

Yeo added: "For Reece to come back in a contest like that with some of those plays is a massive effort after not playing for eight weeks. It won't get spoken about enough but it is really hard to do at this level.

"He has just got the ability to just make people miss. I think he made two people miss on the one move but he's just one of those players that can just break a game open, and we probably needed that."

Australia edge New Zealand in epic World Cup opener

Having finally fulfilled a long-held desire to represent New Zealand, Ponga's night was going sweetly - he scored two tries that included one trademark run from deep and elusive step that left Walsh clutching at air - but it ended on a bitter note.

For one thing, Australia swiped victory from the grasp of Stacey Jones' team. For another, Ponga's futre participation in the World Cup is now in serious doubt.

Speaking after the game, Jones admitted that the Newcastle Knights man would now have medical checks after playing on for a quarter of the contest with an injury sustained in a tackle with Cameron Munster.

"It's a possible fracture of the arm but he's going to go for scans and we're not going to make a call on him right now where he's at," said Jones.

"I think he played on for 20 minutes, he toughed it out. It's a tough one. They scored a try and that's when we were told what it possibly was and that he would have to come off.

"He couldn't catch the ball or anything like that, he was in a lot of discomfort."

Should Ponga be ruled out it would be a huge blow to New Zealand's hopes of winning a second World Cup, 18 years on from their first.

articles.title: Wales aim to punch above weight on Rugby League World Cup debut
articles.summary: Despite a daunting group Wales women's head coach Tom Brindle says the team want to play their part in growing rugby league.
articles.body:
Wales women's head coach Tom Brindle says the team want to play their part in growing rugby league as a "small nation punching above their weight".

His side make the country's Rugby League World Cup debut against England on Saturday in Perth, before facing Samoa and co-hosts Australia in Sydney.

Group A provides a daunting test for a team who played their first full international in June 2021.

"Not only is it a big opportunity for us as Wales and the people of Wales, I think it's a big opportunity for rugby league across Europe," said Brindle.

"We have to pinch ourselves that we set off on a journey and we got here and we're not too far away from competing at our first World Cup game."

Brindle has named a 21-player squad, with three new caps in the starting line-up and two others who could make their debut from the bench.

Hannah Bluck will represent Wales in her fourth sport, having earned 15 senior caps in rugby union as well as representing the country at basketball and U19s level football.

Canterbury Bulldogs captain, Sydney-born Tayla Preston, makes her debut at scrum-half alongside Ffion Lewis at stand-off - who becomes the first Welsh woman to play in a World Cup in both codes.

The other debutant in the Wales starting line-up is St Helens second row Paige Travis, who represented England at the delayed 2021 Rugby League World Cup.

Captain Bethan Dainton says the new faces in the squad have "bought into the culture" of the team.

"They jumped in like they've been part of this team the whole time, you can't tell that they're new to the squad at all," said Dainton.

"We've got strengths all across the park, we've got some other leaders in the squad which will help the team.

"They're amazing athletes as well so I'm excited to see how we go as a team on Saturday."

On the bench is Erin Williams, who is hoping to follow in the footsteps of brother Zak, who also represented Wales in rugby league.

She joined Cardiff Demons midway through their season and could make her international debut in just her sixth match in the sport.

"Following in my brother's footsteps is a massive honour for me, he's a massive inspiration in my life.

"I know I put the work in myself but he's the one who pushed me to play the sport, it's a huge honour.

"It's something I've always dreamed of I just didn't think it would come this early."

World Cup history beckons for Wales' defiant Lewis

Wales had played only nine games before being given a chance to reach the World Cup in Australia - and they took it in style.

They travelled to Netherlands, beating them 48-6 in June 2024 to seal their place at the global gathering.

They had also beaten Ireland 28-10 in Cardiff in their opening qualifier.

But if they needed a reality check, it came in November 2024 in Leeds - an 82-0 humbling by England.

Only two friendlies followed in 2024 - an 18-12 triumph against Scotland followed by another heavy 62-0 defeat by the Lionesses, with both games taking place at Neath's Gnoll ground.

Their build-up before travelling to Australia this autumn was also at the Gnoll, a 14-0 loss to Canada in July.

With an aggregate deficit of 144-0 in two matches against their neighbours to ponder before kicking off the tournament against England in Perth on Saturday, 17 October, Wales already know they face a daunting task.

Samoa present a lesser-known quantity for Wales' second game in Sydney on Friday, 23 October, having last competed at the tournament in 2008.

But then comes the prospect of facing defending champions Australia, also in Sydney, on Sunday, 1 November to complete their Pool A campaign.

Saturday's meeting with England represents just the 14th full international for Brindle's side.

"I'm a big believer that anything takes a decade," said Brindle.

"We're six years into this journey and we're not too far off.

"Another ten years from now, we'll see the impact of this team, Bethan leading the team out on Saturday, but we have to sustain it.

"We know we're in a tough group, we know there's going to be challenges but if we live up to our values, I think we'll grow and be in a better place both in Wales and internationally in ten years time."

Brindle hopes Wales' exploits help to grow the game.

"I firmly believe in the international game, if women's rugby league needs to continue to grow to be successful, we need more internationals, more regularly.

"Over the years that was often driven in the northern hemisphere between France and England.

"I believe our introduction and getting to this point has put more teams on the map and that's helped inspire more teams around like Ireland and Scotland."

"We have girls that now want to be Bethan when they grow up, they're playing more, they're sending us videos, it's inspiring."

Regardless of the result on Saturday, it will be a proud occasion for the squad.

"It's always an honour to represent Wales in any sport," said Dainton.

"But I think to captain your country at a World Cup is going to be special and it's something that nobody can take away from you.

"As soon as we walk out, I think that's when it'll start hitting myself and the girls how big this is and how far we've come from the first game."

articles.title: European Challenge Cup: Ulster 'know how dangerous Zebre can be' - Tom O'Toole
articles.summary: Ulster prop Tom O'Toole says there will be no sense of complacency in the Irish province's ranks when they take on Zebre in their Challenge Cup opener in Parma on Saturday.
articles.body:
Ulster prop Tom O'Toole says the Irish province will take nothing for granted when they travel to Parma to take on Italian side Zebre to open their European Challenge Cup campaign on Saturday (15:15 BST).

Richie Murphy's side have drawn two and lost one of their first three United Rugby Championship [URC] games to kick off the season, while their opponents at Stadio Sergio Lanfranchi this weekend have lost their first three this term.

Having tasted defeat in their past 16 matches of the 2025-26 URC campaign, Zebre are on a 19-game losing streak in that competition.

They did however stun Ulster by winning 15-14 when the sides met in Belfast in January 2025, an outcome which the Ireland front row says will eliminate any sense of complacency in the ranks.

"It's kind of weird having a European game so early in the calendar but it's nice to park the URC for a week and obviously we know Zebre quite well," O'Toole told BBC Sport NI.

"They upset us here a couple of years ago so we realise how dangerous they can be.

"Especially at home they'll be a side that is very physical and probably pride themselves a little bit more at home.

"I think the last few games they've played, the score has been quite tight at half-time, the first 40 minutes of those have been quite tight games, even though they've lost their three games, so we know the challenges going to Italy this week."

Ulster lost at home to Edinburgh in their season opener, before playing out draws away to Glasgow and at home to Munster.

Murphy's charges recovered from a 21-point half-time deficit against Munster to earn a 26-26 result last weekend but will hope their European opener can give them a platform to build on their run to the Challenge Cup final last season, which ended disappointingly with a heavy defeat by Montpellier in the decider.

"It's been a bit disappointing the past couple of weeks ending up with draws, although it's still points for us that we can take away for the URC," added O'Toole.

"Fixing up our discipline is key, to not give teams much access straight from a set-piece.

"There are some penalties we gave away there that were avoidable, a couple of offsides, unfortunately Izzy [Cormac Izuchukwu] got yellow-carded at the weekend, and that came at a pretty costly time for us.

"If we can fix up a few of those mistakes I think we'll be in a much better position."

The 28-year-old will hope to be part of Andy Farrell's Ireland squad for the resumption of the Nations Championship in November as he aims to add to the 24 caps he has won to date.

Argentina, Fiji and South Africa will be their opponents ahead of the finals weekend at the end of November.

Farrell's team beat Australia and Japan in July, before suffering a loss against New Zealand.

"It's very exciting, it's always really nice to reconnect with that group. The opportunity to represent your country is an unbelievable honour.

"We've got a couple of weeks of Ulster games to go until that squad is announced so I just plan to do my best over the next couple of weeks and perform well."

After Saturday's encounter, Ulster will resume their Challenge Cup campaign when they host French side Bayonne at the Affidea Stadium on 12 December.
